tags: neutral: Codex read-aloud; separate codex audio manifest; text = data/codex.json, spoken form
text: Usable delta-v comes from the rocket equation: I-S-P in seconds, times standard gravity, times the natural log of starting mass over final mass. Standard gravity is nine point eight zero six six five meters per second squared. Final mass is starting mass minus usable propellant. A landing reserve is held as dry mass and is not usable. The designer allows at most thirty percent of that stage's propellant as reserve. For a closed orbit, the required delta-v is the speed at periapsis, minus the launch site's rotation speed at twenty-eight point five degrees, plus a flat loss budget of fifteen hundred meters per second. Periapsis speed is the square root of mu, times two over the periapsis radius, minus two over the sum of periapsis and apoapsis radii, with mu equal to three point nine eight six zero zero four four one eight times ten to the fourteenth cubic meters per second squared, and Earth's radius six million three hundred seventy-eight thousand one hundred thirty-seven meters. Site speed there is about four hundred nine meters per second. For a two hundred kilometer orbit, circular speed is about seven thousand seven hundred eighty-four meters per second, and the budget is about eight thousand eight hundred seventy-six. A suborbital target is not a closed orbit. Its budget is the square root of two times g times height, plus one thousand meters per second. The fifteen hundred meter per second term is a flat allowance. The ascent sim's own losses can differ.

tags: neutral: Codex read-aloud; separate codex audio manifest; text = data/codex.json, spoken form
text: Pad thrust-to-weight is the sea-level thrust of the first phase, divided by liftoff mass times standard gravity. Later phases use vacuum thrust. Liftoff mass is the payload, the fairing, and every stage still attached, propellant plus dry mass. The designer blocks the launch unless liftoff thrust-to-weight is strictly above one point zero. A marginal warning fires below one point two five. If losing one engine would drop liftoff thrust-to-weight under one, the designer adds an engine-out warning.

tags: neutral: Codex read-aloud; separate codex audio manifest; text = data/codex.json, spoken form
text: I-S-P is measured in seconds. The game blends the catalog's sea-level and vacuum values by air pressure: vacuum I-S-P, minus the difference between vacuum and sea-level I-S-P, times local pressure over sea-level pressure. Sea-level pressure is one hundred one thousand three hundred twenty-five pascals. Thrust uses the same blend. Mass flow is thrust divided by I-S-P times standard gravity. Each catalog engine's vacuum I-S-P stays at or under its propellant's maximum. The engineer tune can multiply I-S-P by up to fifteen percent, and that product is not clamped to the maximum. The designer's delta-v total uses vacuum I-S-P. The flight sims burn with the blended I-S-P at the local air pressure.

tags: neutral: Codex read-aloud; separate codex audio manifest; text = data/codex.json, spoken form
text: Stages stack from the bottom. For each stage, starting mass is that stage's propellant and dry mass, plus every stage above it, plus payload and fairing. That stage's delta-v is its vacuum I-S-P times standard gravity times the natural log of starting mass over starting mass minus usable propellant. Strap-ons burn beside the core and fold into one phase. Separation mass and interstage mass add to dry mass. An interstage is zero point six times the larger diameter long. Each flare or shoulder adds zero point zero two to the drag coefficient. A straight joint adds none. That mass and drag do not reorder the burns. The fairing drops on its own, by default at one hundred ten kilometers.

The drag coefficient holds its low-speed value up to Mach zero point eight, rises to twice that value at Mach one point one, then falls as Mach climbs.
